[Convention lock and verbatim transfer]
\label{rem:convention}
The reading of the final bracket of \eqref{eq:screw} is fixed by
Suzuki's own Section~2.2: the printed constant
$A=\tfrac12(\log2\pi-\psi(2))=0.707546\ldots$ of \eqref{eq:origin}
holds \emph{only} if the Lerch term carries the coefficient $+\tfrac14$
(machine check: with coefficient $+\tfrac14$ the origin read
reproduces $A$ to $1.2\times10^{-9}$ at $t=10^{-8}$; with coefficient
$-1$ it is off by $\approx56$ and $g(0)=-\tfrac54\Phi(1,2,\tfrac14)
=-21.4967\neq0$).  An earlier tranche of machine verifications (probe
files \texttt{w1\_dictionary\_probe.py},
\texttt{w1\_boundary\_closure\_probe.py},
\texttt{w1\_frozen\_windows\_probe.py},
\texttt{w1\_matrix\_identity\_probe.py}) used the kernel
$\tilde g:=g-\tfrac54e^{-|t|/2}\Phi(e^{-2|t|},2,\tfrac14)$ (Lerch
coefficient $-1$).  Since
$\tilde g_{\mathrm{sm}}''=-4\rho$ while $g_{\mathrm{sm}}''=+\rho$, one
has $c_{\mathrm{gal}}^{\mathrm{sm}}(\tilde g)
=-4\,c_{\mathrm{gal}}^{\mathrm{sm}}(g)$ \emph{exactly} (checked to
$3.7\times10^{-12}$), so every measured ratio of that tranche transfers
verbatim:
$c_{\mathrm{gal}}(\tilde g)/(-4Dc_{\mathrm{ar}})
\equiv c_{\mathrm{gal}}(g)/(+Dc_{\mathrm{ar}})$.  All numbers quoted
below from those probes are therefore valid for the true dictionary;
only the labels change ($-4D$ two-layer $\mapsto$ $+D$ one-scalar, and
the sign of the identification becomes positivity-compatible).

claims.source_body:
[unconditional smoothed-density bound]
\label{cor:fejer}
Let $\rho_{a,\delta}=s_{\mathrm{tot}}\ast\Phi_\delta$ with the
unit-mass Fej\'er kernel $\Phi_\delta$ of main-lobe half-width
$\delta$.  Windowed Riemann--von Mangoldt counting with Trudgian's
bound $|S(t)|\le0.112\log t+0.278\log\log t+2.510$ \cite{Tru14}, the
Fej\'er box minorant and $F_a$ mass transfer give, for
$\delta\in\{4\pi,\pi a\}$ and every family window,
\[
\rho_{a,\delta}(t)\ \ge\ c_0\log(2+t)-C_0\qquad(t\ge t_0(a,\delta)),
\]
with the finite remainder $[10,t_0]$ machine-checked on the zero-free
grids: all $10$ $(a,\delta)$ certificates pass with margins
$\ge+1.36$ (bar $0.05$), $\min c_0=0.3058$, $C_0\le2.50$,
$t_0\le3530$ --- a $15.1\times$ gain over the raw measured hull slope
$0.0202$.  The chain closes \emph{only} above the certifiability floor
$\delta>4\pi\cdot0.112=1.4074$: the literal width $1/a\le0.361$ and
the plane-wave resolution $\pi/a\le1.133$ sit below the floor for
every family window, so per-mode (pointwise) symbol control is not
certifiable this way at any height --- the honest structural
explanation of the measured $1/\log$ G\r{a}rding drift.

Paper-to-declaration domain match
Global bridge separately proved

claims.anchor: \label{thm:rung}
requires: Fine matrix positive definite
Exact nesting
U positive definite and certified majorant
Carried coarse solution
claims.statement: The rung bounds delta by shat-transpose times inverse-U times shat. It assumes fine-level positive definiteness, exact nesting and a certified positive majorant, and uses the carried coarse solution.

claims.source_body:
[the direction, stated pedantically]
\label{rem:direction}
From \eqref{eq:primal}, every test vector yields an \emph{upper} bound on
$\delta_{l}$; a minimum principle cannot supply a lower bound, no matter how good the
test vector. From \eqref{eq:maximum}, every test vector yields a \emph{lower} bound
on $\delta_{l}$, provided the denominator $v^{\T}Sv$ is replaced by something
\emph{larger}. This is the direction reversal of the title of
Section~\ref{sec:main}: what a lower bound on $\delta_{l}$ needs is an
\emph{upper} bound on $S$, and upper bounds on Schur complements are cheap.

claims.source_body:
[what is certifiable, and how]
\label{rem:certify}
Each of \ref{H:pd}--\ref{H:maj} reduces to a completed Cholesky factorisation:
$A^{(l+1)}\PD$ and $U_{l}\PD$ directly, and the majorant property through
$\Tm{M_{l+1}}(\mathrm{up})-\Tm{M_{l+1}}(c)\PSD$, which is
Lemma~\ref{lem:parseval} in the certified direction. In particular
$A_{c}\PSD$ --- the hypothesis whose quantitative version blocks the classical
routes --- is supplied by the previous rung's own conclusion and never has to be
quantified. This is what makes a coarse-to-fine induction possible; see
Corollary~\ref{cor:chain}.

claims.source_body:
[carried-solution accounting]
\label{conv:carried}
The numerator $\shat_{l}=s_{l}-B_{x}^{\T}u^{(l)}$ of \eqref{eq:8R} is a
function of the coarse Galerkin solution $u^{(l)}$ carried along the ladder.
Theorem~\ref{thm:rung} and Corollary~\ref{cor:chain} are therefore statements about
the \emph{carried-solution} rung: given the ladder and its coarse solutions, the
bound is certified. A \emph{solution-free} rung --- one whose right-hand side is
computable from $(c,b,\mathrm{up})$ alone --- is not claimed. See
Proposition~\ref{prop:negative}.

claims.source_body:
[the convention is a scope, not a circularity]
\label{rem:scope}
It is worth being explicit about what Convention~\ref{conv:carried} does and does not
cost, because a bound whose right-hand side involves a solution invites the suspicion
that it presupposes what it proves. It does not: $u^{(l)}$ is the Galerkin solution on
the \emph{coarse} space, computed there, and \eqref{eq:8R} bounds the increment gained
by refining --- so nothing in $\widehat c_{l}$ requires knowing $\varepsilon_{l}$,
$\varepsilon_{l+1}$, or the fine solution $u^{(l+1)}$. This is precisely the
information an a posteriori estimator has available: hierarchical estimators in the
sense of \cite{BankSmith1993,BornemannErdmannKornhuber1996,DorflerNochetto2002}
evaluate a residual against the computed coarse solution and are two-sided only under

convention rules out is a different and stronger object --- an a priori bound in the
data alone --- and Proposition~\ref{prop:negative} measures how far that object is
from reach.

[admissible common resolution]
\label{def:admissible}
Let $u_{i}<u_{i+1}<\dots<u_{j}$ be consecutive comb nodes with log-gaps
$g_{k}=u_{k+1}-u_{k}$, and fix $\nu\ge4$. Put
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:D}
  D=\frac{\min_{k}g_{k}}{2\nu},
  \qquad

Definition~\ref{def:window} at $(D,M_{k})$ with the lag sequence \eqref{eq:lags}.
We call $D$ \emph{admissible} for the run and write $g_{c}^{(k)}=(M_{k+1}-M_{k})/2$
for the window increment per end.

[exact handover identity]
\label{lem:handover}
Let $D>0$, let $M_{o}<M_{n}$ be even with $M_{n}-M_{o}=2g_{c}$, and let
$c^{(o)},c^{(n)}$ be lag sequences with $c^{(n)}_{m}=c^{(o)}_{m}$ for
$0\le m\le M_{o}-1$. Let $A^{(o)},b^{(o)}$ and $A^{(n)},b^{(n)}$ be as in
Definition~\ref{def:window} at $(D,M_{o})$ and $(D,M_{n})$, and write $h_{o}=M_{o}/2$.
Then, with indices $r=g_{c}+r'$, $s=g_{c}+s'$ for $r',s'\in\{0,\dots,h_{o}-1\}$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:handover}
  A^{(n)}_{rs}=A^{(o)}_{r's'},
  \qquad
  b^{(n)}_{r}=b^{(o)}_{r'} .
\end{equation}
Hence the trailing $h_{o}\times h_{o}$ block of $Q^{(n)}=A^{(n)}-b^{(n)}(b^{(n)})^{\T}$
equals $Q^{(o)}$ exactly.

The two lemmas together say that on an admissible run the chain
\emph{composes literally}: by Lemma~\ref{lem:zeroblock} the lag sequences agree on the
old range, so by Lemma~\ref{lem:handover} the trailing block of the next window's
bordered form is the current window's bordered form, not merely close to it. The
coordinate ordering matters and is the natural one: index $r=0$ is the outermost cell,
so a window that grows by $g_{c}$ cells per end acquires its new coordinates at the
\emph{leading} indices.

[where the induction runs, and why it must]
\label{rem:direction2}
The telescope \eqref{eq:sat} places its certified bound on the \emph{coarse} level:
$\varepsilon_{\text{coarse}}=\varepsilon_{\text{fine}}+\delta$ with $\delta\ge0$, so
the target window must be the coarsest level of its chain and the base case
\ref{A:base} sits at the finest. A bound at the fine level would require certified
\emph{upper} bounds on the rungs, i.e.\ a strengthened Cauchy--Schwarz constant, which
is precisely the quantity the construction is built to avoid. This is a structural
feature, not a choice.

[interlacing]
\label{lem:interlacing}
Let $X\in\R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric and $P\in\R^{n\times m}$ an isometry.
Then the eigenvalues of $P^{\T}XP$ interlace those of $X$; in particular
$\lmin(X)\le\lmin(P^{\T}XP)$. Consequently a $K$-truncated Rayleigh minimum is
an upper bound for $\lmin$ and never a lower bound.

[what summation by parts can certify]
\label{cor:holder}
For every admissible $x$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:holder}
  |Q(x)|\;\le\;\Bigl(\max_{0\le d\le M-1}|C_d|\Bigr)\,\TV(x),
  \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
  \max_{d}|C_d|\;\ge\;\frac{|Q(x)|}{\TV(x)} .
\end{equation}
Combined with \eqref{eq:price}, a family of bounded value certifies
$\max_d|C_d|\ge$ a quantity that is $O(h^{-2})$, and nothing stronger. By the
gauge law of Lemma~\ref{lem:gauge} the estimate may be applied to $c+\gamma$ for
any $\gamma\in\R$, so $\max_d|C_d|$ may be replaced by
$\inf_{\gamma}\max_d|C_d+\gamma(d+1)|$.

[sharpness of the floor]
\label{meas:sharpness}
On Surface~II of Section~\ref{sec:numerics} --- $27$ windows of the frame-A
family, $h=142$ to $1445$, all with $\cond(G)\le10^{12}$ --- the floor of
Theorem~\ref{thm:tvfloor} is tight to about one order of magnitude: the measured
ratio is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:sharp}
  \mu_1\,\TV(x)\in[5.00,\ 23.20]
\end{equation}
at the optimiser of the declared trial family, while the floor itself takes the
values $2.06\cdot10^{3}$ to $1.77\cdot10^{5}$, growing as $h^{+1.997}$ (a
least-squares fit, reported for orientation and not used anywhere) against the
closed $h^{2}$ of \eqref{eq:gap}. The inadmissible control of
Remark~\ref{rem:negcontrol} returns $\mu_1\TV\approx7\cdot10^{-4}$ at
$\lambda=10^{-2}$, i.e.\ it undercuts the floor by the predicted factor
$\lambda^{2}$.
The trial family is the declared tapered mode family also used in
Measurement~\ref{meas:battery}, its taper width running over a fixed geometric
list; the caps of Surface~II are written out in Section~\ref{sec:surfaces}.

[the null mode, and the other sector]
\label{prop:nullmode}
Let $c^{L}=(2,-1,0,\dots)$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:kms}.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.6em]
\item\label{N:sine} The parity family $\mu_k=4\sin^{2}(k\pi/N)$,
  $k=1,\dots,h$, is the restriction to $k\ge1$ of the sine family
  $\{4\sin^{2}(k\pi/N)\}_{k\ge0}$, whose member at $k=0$ is $\mu_0=0$.
\item\label{N:noreps} The parametrisation $a_k=x_k/\sqrt{\mu'_k}$ of
  Theorem~\ref{thm:gauge}\ref{G:gauge} requires $\mu'_k>0$. If a mode family
  containing a null mode is used and the normalisation is imposed on that mode,
  the constraint has \emph{no} representative $a$ of finite norm; if the
  normalisation is imposed elsewhere, step (iii) of
  Theorem~\ref{thm:tvfloor} yields the floor of the normalised mode and the
  null mode contributes nothing. In neither case is a flatter admissible floor
  obtained.
\item\label{N:even} Write $\Pi_+e_r=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(e_r+e_{M-1-r})$ for the
  reflection-even isometry. The complementary compression
  $\Pi_+^{\T}\Tm{M}(c^{L})\Pi_+$ has spectrum
  $\bigl\{4\sin^{2}\bigl((2k+1)\pi/(2N)\bigr)\bigr\}_{k=0}^{h-1}$, whose
  minimum $4\sin^{2}(\pi/(2N))$ is \emph{strictly smaller} than $\mu_1$. Hence
  no reflection sector of the second-difference form has a lowest eigenvalue
  exceeding $\mu_1$.
\end{enumerate}

claims.source_body:
\label{rem:onedress}
Proposition~\ref{prop:union} is the reason the three natural readings of the
same obstruction --- a determinant ratio, the scalar $1-r_{12}^{2}$, and an
entrywise perturbation threshold --- are one object rather than three: at $k=2$
they differ by the explicit factor $1+3r_{12}^{2}\in[1,4]$. We state the two
formulae and leave the reading to the reader; ``three dresses of one
inequality'' is an observation about identities, not a theorem.

claims.source_body:
[observation: the section is a closed loop]
\label{rem:selfsimilar}
Every statement of this section is an \emph{identity} --- with the single
exception of the Gershgorin bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:gershgorin}, which is an
inequality about $\nu_1$ and not about $\nu_2$, and of the second half of
Proposition~\ref{prop:collapse}, which carries a named hypothesis. Reading them
together:
\begin{itemize}
\item the constrained minimum at $K=2$ is $G_{11}(1-r_{12}^{2})$
  (Proposition~\ref{prop:K2}), so the value of the optimal trial vector is the
  scalar $1-r_{12}^{2}$ up to the closed factor $G_{11}$;
\item that scalar is the normalised determinant
  $\det\Ah_2/(\ah_{11}\ah_{22})$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:detread}), with no positivity
  used;
\item the entrywise perturbation threshold is the same scalar up to the factor
  $1+3r_{12}^{2}\in[1,4]$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:union});
\item the only member of the Rayleigh family $u(t)=(t,-1)$ that meets the
  threshold, $t^{\star}=\sqrt{\ah_{22}/\ah_{11}}$, reintroduces
  $\det\Ah_2$ exactly (Proposition~\ref{prop:collapse});
\item and the Wronskian and Lagrange identities
  (Lemmata~\ref{lem:wronskian}--\ref{lem:minors}) say that none of the
  smallness can be attributed to the two modes.
\end{itemize}
Consequently \emph{no stage of the reduction lowers the accuracy demanded of
$\det\Ah_2$}: the four readings differ by the explicit factors $G_{11}$,
$\ah_{11}\ah_{22}$, $1+3r_{12}^{2}$ and the closed prefactor of
\eqref{eq:collapse}, all of which are computable from the three entries and
none of which is small. We record this as an \emph{observation} about a family
of identities, not as a theorem: it is a reading, the statement ``every exact
reformulation costs the same precision'' quantifies over reformulations rather
than over windows, and how much precision is in fact demanded is a measured
number that belongs in Section~\ref{sec:open}.

claims.source_body:
[the wedge form of the kernel, under exact rank one]
\label{lem:wedge}
Write $x\wedge x'=x_1x'_2-x_2x'_1$ for $x,x'\in\R^{2}$. If every read is of
rank one, $X^{(\ell)}=\epsilon_\ell\,x_\ell x_\ell^{\T}$ with
$\epsilon_\ell\in\{\pm1\}$ and $x_\ell\in\R^{2}$, then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:wedge}
  \mathcal K(\ell,\ell')
  =\tfrac12\,\epsilon_\ell\epsilon_{\ell'}\,
  \bigl(x_\ell\wedge x_{\ell'}\bigr)^{2} .
\end{equation}
In particular the diagonal vanishes, $\mathcal K(\ell,\ell)=0$, and the sign
pattern of $\mathcal K$ is exactly that of $\epsilon_\ell\epsilon_{\ell'}$ ---
mixed as soon as the $\epsilon_\ell$ are not all equal. The hypothesis is
equivalent to $\det X^{(\ell)}=0$ for every $\ell$ and is \emph{not} an
identity: Measurement~\ref{meas:l1} reports how far from it the reads are.

claims.source_body:
[what a majorant of the comb--comb term can see]
\label{cor:majorant}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.6em]
\item\label{M:bound} If \eqref{eq:majclass} holds then necessarily
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:majorant}
  \Phi(t)\;\ge\;\sup\bigl\{|y_1y_2-y_3^{2}|:\ y\in\R^{3},\
  y=\bigl(S_{11},S_{22},S_{12}\bigr)\ \text{for some }\varrho\ \text{with }
  \mathcal N(\varrho)\le t\bigr\}.
\end{equation}
\item\label{M:blind} Consequently no member of $\mathfrak M$ distinguishes two
  weight vectors with the same image $y(S)=(S_{11},S_{22},S_{12})$, and every
  cancellation between the three terms of \eqref{eq:polarisation} is invisible
  to it: the bound sees a point of $\R^{3}$, the phenomenon is a relation
  between that point and $B$.
\item\label{M:decomp} If a route proceeds through a declared linear
  decomposition $\varrho=\sum_{q\le p}\varrho^{(q)}$ and bounds
  $|\det S|\le\sum_{q,q'}\Phi_{qq'}\bigl(\mathcal N(\varrho^{(q)}),
  \mathcal N(\varrho^{(q')})\bigr)$ with each $\Phi_{qq'}$ nondecreasing in
  both arguments, then each summand obeys the analogue of \ref{M:bound} for the
  corresponding block of the bilinear form, and the total pays in addition the
  triangle inequality across the $p^{2}$ pairs --- whose cost is measured in
  Measurement~\ref{meas:l1}.
\end{enumerate}

claims.source_body:
[the five declared routes, classified]
\label{rem:routeclass}
Of the five preregistered routes of Measurement~\ref{meas:routes}, three are
members of $\mathfrak M$ as they are stated: the large-sieve/duality route, with
$\mathcal N=\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ and
$\Phi(t)=\lVert\mathcal K\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}t^{2}$; the
Montgomery--Vaughan route, which bounds each of the three linear functionals
through $\lVert\varrho\rVert_2$ --- its interpolation residual through
$\lVert\varrho\rVert_1\le\sqrt n\,\lVert\varrho\rVert_2$ on a window with $n$
nodes, so that one norm suffices --- and then combines them by
$|\det S|\le|S_{11}||S_{22}|+S_{12}^{2}$; and the comb--comb term of the exact
split $|\det B|+|D(B,S)|+|\det S|$. Vaughan's Type~I $+$ Type~II route is of
the shape of Corollary~\ref{cor:majorant}\ref{M:decomp} with $p=4$. The
remaining route, Cauchy--Schwarz on $\Ah_2$, is not a majorant of $\det S$ at
all: it asserts $\ah_{12}^{2}\le\ah_{11}\ah_{22}$, i.e.\ $\det\Ah_2\ge0$, and
is carried in the table as the trivial baseline. This classification is a
\emph{reading of the five routes as declared}, not a theorem about every
conceivable implementation of them; what is a theorem is
Corollary~\ref{cor:majorant} itself.

claims.source_body:
[mixed signs, and what the triangle inequality costs]
\label{meas:l1}
Two numbers price the two hypotheses just used. \emph{The rank-one defect}: the
median of $|\det X^{(\ell)}|/\lVert X^{(\ell)}\rVert^{2}$ over the nodes is
$1.3\cdot10^{-4}$ on the reference window of
Measurement~\ref{meas:refwindow}, and on Surface~I it lies between
$4.6\cdot10^{-3}$ and $3.1\cdot10^{-2}$, below the declared bar
$5\cdot10^{-2}$ on every window. So the wedge reading of
Lemma~\ref{lem:wedge} is accurate but not exact --- the diagonal of
$\mathcal K$ is small, not zero, and it carries about $6\%$ of $\det S$ on the
reference window. \emph{The $\ell^{1}$ mass}: on a declared node
subsample of the reference window,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:l1mass}
  \sum_{\ell,\ell'}\varrho_\ell\varrho_{\ell'}
  \bigl|\mathcal K(\ell,\ell')\bigr|
  \;=\;40.6\times
  \Bigl|\sum_{\ell,\ell'}\varrho_\ell\varrho_{\ell'}
  \mathcal K(\ell,\ell')\Bigr| ,
\end{equation}
the subsample being the $900$ nodes of the declared horizon and the ratio being
reported on the window it was computed on and on no other. A
route that replaces the signed double sum by its absolute value therefore loses
that factor before it begins, which is the measured content of
Corollary~\ref{cor:majorant}\ref{M:decomp}; the mixed signs it loses are the
ones Lemma~\ref{lem:wedge} and Theorem~\ref{thm:rank3}\ref{R:inertia} predict.

claims.source_body:
[the weight sequence has bandwidth $K$ and degree one]
\label{lem:band}
Let $\mathcal V_K\subset\R^{M-1}$ be the span of the $4K$ sequences
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bandspace}
  d\mapsto\cos(\omega_kd),\quad \sin(\omega_kd),\quad
  d\cos(\omega_kd),\quad d\sin(\omega_kd),
  \qquad k=1,\dots,K,\ 1\le d\le M-1 .
\end{equation}
Then $\bigl(w_d(v)\bigr)_{d=1}^{M-1}\in\mathcal V_K$ for every
$v\in\operatorname{span}\{t_1,\dots,t_K\}$, and consequently also for every
polarised weight vector $w^{(ij)}$ of \eqref{eq:Yread} with $i,j\le K$. The
coefficients of $d\cos(\omega_kd)$ and $d\sin(\omega_kd)$ are proportional to
$a_k^{2}$, where $v=\sum_ka_kt_k$.

claims.source_body:
[the two-point read against the analytic read]
\label{lem:spline}
Let $v\in\operatorname{span}\{t_1,\dots,t_K\}$ and let $W_v$ be the function
obtained by evaluating the representation of Lemma~\ref{lem:band} at real
argument, so that $W_v(d)=w_d(v)$ for integers $1\le d\le M-1$. For
$1\le\tau\le M-1$ the two-point read
$\widehat W_v(\tau)=(1-\theta)w_{m}(v)+\theta w_{m+1}(v)$,
$m=\lfloor\tau\rfloor$, $\theta=\tau-m$, of \eqref{eq:split} satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:splinebound}
  \sup_{1\le\tau\le M-1}\bigl|\widehat W_v(\tau)-W_v(\tau)\bigr|
  \;\le\;\tfrac18\sup_{1\le\tau\le M-1}|W_v''(\tau)|
  \;\le\;\tfrac18\bigl[\omega_K^{2}\Lambda_0+2\omega_K\Lambda_1\bigr],
\end{equation}
where $\Lambda_0=\sum_k(|\alpha_k|+|\gamma_k|+M(|\beta_k|+|\delta_k|))$ and
$\Lambda_1=\sum_k(|\beta_k|+|\delta_k|)$ in the notation
$W_v(\tau)=\sum_k[(\alpha_k+\beta_k\tau)\cos(\omega_k\tau)
+(\gamma_k+\delta_k\tau)\sin(\omega_k\tau)]$. For the single mode $t_k$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:splinemode}
  \sup_{1\le\tau\le M-1}\bigl|\widehat W_{t_k}(\tau)-W_{t_k}(\tau)\bigr|
  \;\le\;\frac{\pi^{2}k^{2}}{N^{2}}\Bigl(1+\frac3{2\pi k}\Bigr)
  \;=\;O\!\left(\frac{k^{2}}{N^{2}}\right).
\end{equation}

claims.source_body:
[$\eta$-rank of a factorisation-indexed block]
\label{prop:typeII}
Fix $K$, let the weight vector be either $w(v)$ for some
$v\in\operatorname{span}\{t_1,\dots,t_K\}$ or a polarised $w^{(ij)}$ with
$i,j\le K$, and let $\widehat W$ be its two-point read as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:spline}. Let $\mathcal B_1,\mathcal B_2$ be two finite sets of
reals $>1$, put $x_{b_1}=\log b_1/D$, $y_{b_2}=\log b_2/D$, and assume the block
is \emph{interior}:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:interior}
  1\le x_{b_1}+y_{b_2}\le M-1
  \qquad\text{for all } b_1\in\mathcal B_1,\ b_2\in\mathcal B_2 .
\end{equation}
Then the matrix of reads
$F_{b_1b_2}=\widehat W\bigl(x_{b_1}+y_{b_2}\bigr)$, $R=|\mathcal B_1|$,
$C=|\mathcal B_2|$, satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:typeIIrank}
  \sigma_{4K+1}(F)\;\le\;\eta\sqrt{RC},
  \qquad
  \eta=\tfrac18\sup_{1\le\tau\le M-1}|W''| ,
\end{equation}
with $\eta$ bounded by \eqref{eq:splinebound}; for a single mode
$\eta\le\pi^{2}k^{2}N^{-2}(1+3/(2\pi k))$. The same bound holds for
$\diag(\alpha)F\diag(\beta)$ with $\eta$ replaced by
$\eta\lVert\alpha\rVert_2\lVert\beta\rVert_2$, so arithmetic coefficients
attached to the two index sets do not change the rank count.

$F_{b_1b_2}=\widehat W\bigl(x_{b_1}+y_{b_2}\bigr)$, $R=|\mathcal B_1|$,
$C=|\mathcal B_2|$, satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:typeIIrank}
  \sigma_{4K+1}(F)\;\le\;\eta\sqrt{RC},
  \qquad
  \eta=\tfrac18\sup_{1\le\tau\le M-1}|W''| ,
\end{equation}
with $\eta$ bounded by \eqref{eq:splinebound}; for a single mode
$\eta\le\pi^{2}k^{2}N^{-2}(1+3/(2\pi k))$. The same bound holds for
$\diag(\alpha)F\diag(\beta)$ with $\eta$ replaced by
$\eta\lVert\alpha\rVert_2\lVert\beta\rVert_2$, so arithmetic coefficients
attached to the two index sets do not change the rank count.

[what \eqref{eq:interior} costs, and what the proposition does not
say]
\label{rem:interior}
Hypothesis \eqref{eq:interior} is not cosmetic. Outside the window the weights
are set to zero ($w_m:=0$ for $m\ge M$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:split}), and the
truncation $\mathbf 1[x+y\le M-1]$ is a triangular cut-off, which is \emph{not}
of low rank: without \eqref{eq:interior} the conclusion is false as stated, and
what survives is the same bound for the interior sub-block plus the cut-off
part. On the declared surfaces the node cap makes the block interior by
construction, and that is how the hypothesis is met. Two further limits are
worth naming. The bound \eqref{eq:typeIIrank} is a statement about $4K$ singular
values with a declared $\eta$; it is not a statement that the block ``has rank
$O(1)$'' in any asymptotic sense, and the $\sqrt{RC}$ factor means that the
useful regime is $\eta\sqrt{RC}\ll\sigma_1(F)$, which is a condition on the
declared surface and is checked there, not here. And the whole mechanism is
about \emph{additivity} of the lag argument under factorisation: it uses that
the read happens at $\tau=u/D$ with $u=\log n$, so that $n=b_1b_2$ gives
$\tau=x_{b_1}+y_{b_2}$. Nothing arithmetic beyond that additivity is used, and
nothing is claimed about any Type~II sum beyond the singular values of its
weight matrix.

closed weights, with $K=2$ so that the proved bound is $\sigma_9\le\eta\sqrt{RC}$

generic kernel of the same size, over the scanned range of the decomposition
parameter; the four-term identity for $\Lambda$ is verified coefficientwise
first. The number $2$ is measured and stays measured: the theorem gives $8$ at
$K=2$, the observed sufficiency of $2$ is a property of the declared surface and
is not proved here.

[the reference window: a three-term cancellation]
\label{meas:refwindow}
On the reference window $h=540$, with the comb truncated at the node cap
$2.465\cdot10^{4}$, the three terms of \eqref{eq:polarisation} are
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:refwindow}
  \det B=6.18,
  \qquad
  -D(B,S)=-198.8,
  \qquad
  \det S=192.6,
  \qquad
  \text{sum}=4.22\cdot10^{-3},
\end{equation}
i.e.\ five orders of magnitude of cancellation between three pieces of size
$\approx200$; the absolute value demanded of $\det\Ah_2$ at that window --- the
target against which the cancellation has to be resolved --- is
$1.10\cdot10^{-5}$, a further factor $384$ below the residual sum. The four
numbers are read under the per-window near-null convention \ref{F:null}, and the
caps are those of Surface~II
(Section~\ref{sec:surfaces}): the window index inside $[142,1445]$, the
conditioning of the raw Gram block inside $\cond(G)\le10^{12}$, and the comb
truncated at the node cap quoted above. Three readings of the same window follow
from the results of this section and are recorded as part of the measurement:
the cancellation is between the three terms of the exact polarisation
\eqref{eq:polarisation}, so no route of Definition~\ref{def:majclass} sees it
(Corollary~\ref{cor:majorant}\ref{M:blind}); the signed kernel sum behind
$\det S$ is $40.6$ times smaller than its $\ell^{1}$ mass on the declared
subsample
(Measurement~\ref{meas:l1}); and the sum in \eqref{eq:refwindow} is
$\det\Ah_2$, whose normalisation by $\ah_{11}\ah_{22}$ is the quantity of
Problem~\ref{prob:R1} --- so five orders of magnitude here is a statement about
one window and about nothing else.

[measured rates]
\label{meas:rate}
All numbers here are least-squares fits of $\log$ of the quantity against
$\log h$ on the stated finite surface, reported for orientation and used as
bounds nowhere. On Surface~II of Section~\ref{sec:surfaces} the readings are:
\begin{itemize}
\item $1-r_{12}^{2}\sim h^{-2.747}$ on the $67$ node-complete windows,
  $h=142$ to $1433$;
\item $1-r_{12}^{2}\sim h^{-2.260}$ on the full family of $70$ windows,
  $h=142$ to $1445$, i.e.\ including the $3$ windows whose comb is truncated by
  the node cap. Both numbers are quoted; the difference is the cap, not the
  phenomenon, and it is not hidden;
\item the angle reading of Problem~\ref{prob:R1}\ref{R1:rows},
  $\sin\angle=|\det\Ah_2|/(\rho_1\rho_2)$, falls as $h^{-2.711}$ on the same
  $67$ windows;
\item on the $27$-window frame ladder of Measurements~\ref{meas:sharpness} and
  \ref{meas:battery} the fitted exponent is $-2.921$; on the union of that
  ladder with the decoupled families below it is $-2.246$.
\end{itemize}
The exponent is \emph{not} a single number across surfaces, and this is reported
without smoothing. On three independently generated frames obtained by
decoupling the cell width from the window index the fitted exponents are
$-1.702$, $-1.270$ and $-1.735$, while the best priced route of
Measurement~\ref{meas:routes} certifies $+0.529$, $+0.339$ and $+0.611$ there
--- short of the exponent in \eqref{eq:R1} by $1.17$, $0.93$ and $1.12$. On five
further frame data the pooled exponents are $-2.19$, $-2.46$, $-2.55$, $-1.83$
and $-2.76$, and across the nine individual ladders of those families they
range from $-1.83$ to $-2.87$. What does transfer is the near-degeneracy itself:
the row angle stays below $10^{-2}$ on every window of every family and decays
on every ladder. The rate is a property of the family; the collapse is not.
Nothing in Sections~\ref{sec:setting}--\ref{sec:rank} depends on any of these
numbers.

[five unconditional majorants]
\label{prop:routes}
Let $\Ah_2=B-S$ be the split of Proposition~\ref{prop:split}, let
$\mathcal K$ be the kernel of \eqref{eq:doublesum}, let $\varrho$ be the weight
vector and $\lVert\varrho\rVert_2$ its Euclidean norm. Assume
$\ah_{11}\ah_{22}\ne0$ and write $\Xi=|\ah_{11}\ah_{22}|$ for the length of
this proposition only. Then, with
$1-r_{12}^{2}=\det\Ah_2/(\ah_{11}\ah_{22})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:detread}:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(R\arabic*)},leftmargin=3.2em]
\item\label{RT:cs} \emph{Cauchy--Schwarz on $\Ah_2$.}
  $|\det\Ah_2|\le|\ah_{11}\ah_{22}|+\ah_{12}^{2}$, hence
  $|1-r_{12}^{2}|\le1+\ah_{12}^{2}/\Xi\le2$ whenever $\Ah_2\PSD$. Hypotheses:
  none for the first inequality; $\Ah_2\PSD$ for the numerical bound $2$.
\item\label{RT:ls} \emph{Large sieve / duality on the comb--comb term.}
  $|\det S|\le\lVert\mathcal K\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert\varrho\rVert_2^{2}$,
  hence
  $|1-r_{12}^{2}|\le\bigl[|\det B|+|D(B,S)|
  +\lVert\mathcal K\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\lVert\varrho\rVert_2^{2}\bigr]/\Xi$.
  Hypotheses: $\mathcal K$ symmetric, which is
  Proposition~\ref{prop:polarisation}; the operator-norm step is the Rayleigh
  bound and is the form in which the large sieve enters
  \cite{MontgomeryVaughan1974}.
\item\label{RT:mv} \emph{Montgomery--Vaughan on the three linear functionals.}
  On the prime-power instance with interior reads, Lemma~\ref{lem:dualpoint}
  identifies the three reads as values of one exponential sum of length $X$, and
  of its first logarithmic moment, at the two points $\gamma_k=2\pi k/(ND)$ of
  spacing $\Delta\gamma=2\pi/(ND)$, and gives $|S_{ij}|\le\Qt$ with
  \begin{equation}
  \label{eq:Qtilde}
    \Qt=\Lambda_0\,Q+\eta\lVert\varrho\rVert_1,
    \qquad
    Q^{2}=\bigl(X+\Delta\gamma^{-1}\bigr)\lVert\varrho\rVert_2^{2},
  \end{equation}
  where $\Lambda_0=\max_{ij}\Lambda_0^{(ij)}$ and $\eta=\max_{ij}\eta^{(ij)}$
  are the coefficient budget and the interpolation bound of that lemma. Then
  $|1-r_{12}^{2}|\le\bigl[|\det B|
  +(|B_{11}|+|B_{22}|+2|B_{12}|)\,\Qt+2\Qt^{2}\bigr]/\Xi$. Hypotheses: those of
  Lemma~\ref{lem:dualpoint}, the Montgomery--Vaughan inequality
  \cite{MontgomeryVaughan1974} at the two points that lemma derives, and the
  triangle inequality on $\det S=S_{11}S_{22}-S_{12}^{2}$.
\item\label{RT:split} \emph{The exact split.}
  $|1-r_{12}^{2}|\le\bigl[|\det B|+|D(B,S)|+|\det S|\bigr]/\Xi$. Hypotheses:
  the identity \eqref{eq:polarisation} and the triangle inequality; nothing
  else.
\item\label{RT:vaughan} \emph{Vaughan Type I $+$ Type II.} Write
  $\varrho=\sum_{q\le4}\varrho^{(q)}$ for Vaughan's decomposition
  \cite{Vaughan1977} of the weight vector and bound each of the sixteen
  resulting blocks of the bilinear form by its own operator norm as in
  \ref{RT:ls}. Then
  $|1-r_{12}^{2}|\le\bigl[|\det B|+|D(B,S)|
  +\sum_{q,q'}\lVert\mathcal K\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}
  \lVert\varrho^{(q)}\rVert_2\lVert\varrho^{(q')}\rVert_2\bigr]/\Xi$.
  Hypotheses: those of \ref{RT:ls} for each block, plus
  Corollary~\ref{cor:majorant}\ref{M:decomp}.
\end{enumerate}
Routes \ref{RT:ls}, \ref{RT:mv} and \ref{RT:split} are members of the class
$\mathfrak M$ of Definition~\ref{def:majclass} as stated;
\ref{RT:vaughan} is of the decomposed shape of
Corollary~\ref{cor:majorant}\ref{M:decomp} with $p=4$; \ref{RT:cs} is not a
majorant of $\det S$ at all and is carried as the trivial baseline
(Remark~\ref{rem:routeclass}).

[the priced table]
\label{meas:routes}
Each majorant of Proposition~\ref{prop:routes} is evaluated window by window on
the $67$ node-complete windows of Surface~II and its logarithm regressed against
$\log h$. The resulting $\delta$ is the exponent that the route certifies for
$1-r_{12}^{2}\le C\,h^{-\delta}$ on that surface: the bound is proved, the
exponent is a fit, and the two are typed separately in every row.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{@{}llrY@{}}
\toprule
route & where & $\delta$ & type of the row \\
\midrule
$1-r_{12}^{2}$ itself & Meas.~\ref{meas:rate}
  & $+2.747$ & measured (the object, not a route) \\
\ref{RT:cs} Cauchy--Schwarz on $\Ah_2$ & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $-0.000$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\ref{RT:ls} large sieve / duality on $\det S$ & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $+0.669$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\ref{RT:mv} Montgomery--Vaughan on $S_{11},S_{22},S_{12}$
  & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $-0.384$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\ref{RT:split} exact split $|\det B|+|D(B,S)|+|\det S|$
  & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $+0.996$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\ref{RT:vaughan} Vaughan Type~I $+$ Type~II & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $+0.669$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{center}

\noindent
Row \ref{RT:mv} is priced on the bare Montgomery--Vaughan factor $Q$ of
\eqref{eq:Qtilde}, i.e.\ at $\Lambda_0=1$ and $\eta=0$; the coefficient budget
and the interpolation residual of Lemma~\ref{lem:dualpoint} are window-dependent
prefactors of that factor, and the exponent in the row is the exponent of $Q$ on
this surface. Every other row is priced on the majorant exactly as displayed.

The best of the five on this surface is the triangle inequality on the exact
three-term split, at $\delta=+0.996$; the exponent in \eqref{eq:R1} is $3$, so
on this surface the best priced route falls short by $2.004$ \emph{in the
exponent}. Two readings are part of the measurement.
Corollary~\ref{cor:majorant}\ref{M:blind} says why the three norm-based rows
cannot do better in principle: they see the image point
$y(S)=(S_{11},S_{22},S_{12})$ and not its relation to $B$, and the phenomenon
of Measurement~\ref{meas:refwindow} is exactly that relation.
Theorem~\ref{thm:rank3}\ref{R:three} says why \ref{RT:ls} and \ref{RT:vaughan}
land on the same number: a bilinear tool applied to a kernel of rank three
degenerates to a statement about three linear functionals, and the Vaughan
blocks inherit the degeneracy block by block.

\ref{RT:cs} Cauchy--Schwarz on $\Ah_2$ & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $-0.000$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\ref{RT:ls} large sieve / duality on $\det S$ & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $+0.669$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\ref{RT:mv} Montgomery--Vaughan on $S_{11},S_{22},S_{12}$
  & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $-0.384$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\ref{RT:split} exact split $|\det B|+|D(B,S)|+|\det S|$
  & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}
  & $+0.996$ & bound proved, exponent measured \\
\ref{RT:vaughan} Vaughan Type~I $+$ Type~II & Prop.~\ref{prop:routes}

and the interpolation residual of Lemma~\ref{lem:dualpoint} are window-dependent
prefactors of that factor, and the exponent in the row is the exponent of $Q$ on
this surface. Every other row is priced on the majorant exactly as displayed.

three-term split, at $\delta=+0.996$; the exponent in \eqref{eq:R1} is $3$, so

exponent}. Two readings are part of the measurement.

degenerates to a statement about three linear functionals, and the Vaughan
blocks inherit the degeneracy block by block.

claims.source_body:
[the structural obstructions]
\label{meas:nogo}
Five further routes are excluded not by their exponent but by their shape. Each
is exhibited failing on the windows of Surface~I
(Section~\ref{sec:surfaces}), $12$ windows with $m\le300$, in the way the
classification predicts.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(N\arabic*)},leftmargin=3.2em]
\item\label{NG:symbol} \emph{The symbol infimum is negative.} The Toeplitz
  symbol $\sigma(\theta)=c_0+2\sum_{d\ge1}c_d\cos(d\theta)$ has
  $\min_\theta\sigma\in[-47.6,-21.3]$ on $12/12$ windows, while the parity
  compression is positive definite there. No pointwise minorant of the symbol
  can therefore deliver a positive floor: the positivity is a finite-section
  fact --- a Fej\'er cancellation \cite{Fejer1916} between the Toeplitz and the
  Hankel half of \eqref{eq:Adef} --- and not a symbol fact.
\item\label{NG:kato} \emph{Perturbation theory prices at the wrong scale.}
  Kato's bound $|\nu_2(\Ah_2+E)-\nu_2(\Ah_2)|\le\lVert E\rVert$ \cite{Kato1949}
  is sharp at the scale of the matrix, and on Surface~I the small eigenvalue
  sits a factor $9.8\cdot10^{2}$ to $2.0\cdot10^{4}$ below
  $\lVert\Ah_2\rVert$. A perturbative argument would have to control the matrix
  to that relative accuracy first, which is the original problem. The
  observation is sharper than a divergence statement: on a declared family of
  perturbative expansions the Neumann/Jacobi series diverges (radius $1.0$ to
  $12.7$) while the Kato series \emph{converges}, with radius $0.067$ --- to the
  wrong object, since the exact bottom eigenvector of the corresponding
  $6\times6$ block overshoots the constrained minimum by a relative excess
  $6.04$ at overlap $0.083$ and relative gap $5.4\cdot10^{-7}$.
\item\label{NG:band} \emph{Band-local domination fails.} On the mode-$1$ weight
  vector the comb half of the lag sum dominates the archimedean half by a
  factor $1.71$ to $2.83$ on $12/12$ windows, so a route that would dominate the
  comb band by the archimedean band loses on the instance.
\item\label{NG:l1} \emph{The signed sum is far below its $\ell^{1}$ mass.} On
  the declared subsample of the reference window the ratio is $40.6$
  (Measurement~\ref{meas:l1}, equation~\eqref{eq:l1mass}); any route that
  replaces the signed double sum by its absolute value pays that factor before
  it starts.
\item\label{NG:LP} \emph{The $L_P$ control is exact and empty.} Replacing the
  comb by nothing --- i.e.\ running the whole reduction on the lag sequence
  $c^{L}$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:kms} --- gives $\ah_{12}=1.1\cdot10^{-17}$, hence
  $1-r_{12}^{2}=1$ with no decay at all at $m=64$, $128$ and $256$, a Gram
  matrix that is diagonal to an off-diagonal mass $2.3\cdot10^{-13}$, and a
  ladder gain $g_K/g_1=1$ at zero tolerance. Any argument
  that would already work for $L_P$ alone is therefore vacuous for $A$: the
  phenomenon of Problem~\ref{prob:R1} is not a property of the two parity modes.
\end{enumerate}

claims.source_body:
[the ratio and its binned exponent]
\label{def:ratio}
For a window put
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:ratio}
  \gamma=\frac{\lmin(G)}{\lmax(G)},
  \qquad
  R=\frac{\gamma}{\,1-r_{12}^{2}\,},
  \qquad
  \mathrm{dens}=\frac{\#\{\ell:u_\ell\le2\alpha\}}{M},
\end{equation}
with $G$ the normalised $K$-block of \eqref{eq:gram} at $K=16$ and
$\mathrm{dens}$ the number of comb nodes per lag cell. For a density interval
$[\lambda,4\lambda)$ the \emph{binned exponent} is: for each anchor with at
least three ladder rungs inside the interval, the ordinary least-squares slope
of $\log|R|$ against $\log h$ over its rungs; then the unweighted mean of the
anchor slopes, with the cluster-robust standard error of that mean, and with the
sign reversed so that a positive value means that $R$ falls. The procedure is
deterministic and independent of the order in which the cells are enumerated.

claims.source_body:
[the density curve]
\label{meas:density}
Surface~III of Section~\ref{sec:surfaces}: $692$ anchors, $14\,532$ windows, a
node table capped at $2.5\cdot10^{7}$ containing $1\,566\,727$ nodes, every
window with a complete comb, none of them indefinite. The cap and the smallest
admissible rung force $\mathrm{dens}\le6120$, of which $6118$ is attained; the
attained density spans $4.0$ decades. On the declared geometric ladder of
ratio-$4$ density bins, fixed before any window was built, the binned exponent
of Definition~\ref{def:ratio} is:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrcc@{}}
\toprule
bin (nodes per lag cell) & cells & anchors & exponent $\pm$ s.e.
  & on the $\sqrt2$ sub-ladder \\
\midrule
$[0.1,\ 0.4)$        &   $83$ &  $11$ & $+0.8886\pm0.1027$
  & $+0.9818\pm0.2129$ \\
$[0.4,\ 1.6)$        &  $318$ &  $34$ & $+0.5148\pm0.0883$
  & $+0.5762\pm0.0743$ \\
$[1.6,\ 6.4)$        &  $597$ &  $69$ & $+0.1948\pm0.0861$
  & $+0.2073\pm0.0679$ \\
$[6.4,\ 25.6)$       & $1056$ & $117$ & $+0.3922\pm0.0935$
  & $+0.1942\pm0.0734$ \\
$[25.6,\ 102.4)$     & $1924$ & $218$ & $+0.1520\pm0.0573$
  & $+0.0879\pm0.0589$ \\
$[102.4,\ 409.6)$    & $3588$ & $403$ & $+0.0579\pm0.0542$
  & $-0.0573\pm0.1320$ \\
$[409.6,\ 1638.4)$   & $4891$ & $471$ & $+0.0376\pm0.0410$
  & --- \\
$[1638.4,\ 6553.6)$  & $2075$ & $272$ & $+0.1046\pm0.0881$
  & --- \\
\midrule
pooled, the two densest bins & & & $+0.0496\pm0.0372$ & --- \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent
Every band is the cluster-robust standard error of
Definition~\ref{def:ratio}, the cluster being the anchor; the pooled row is the
inverse-variance pool of the last two bins. Read against zero, the eight bins
sit at $8.7$, $5.8$, $2.3$, $4.2$, $2.7$, $1.1$, $0.9$ and $1.2$ standard
errors, and the pool of the last two at $1.3$. The joint slope of the binned
exponent against $\log(\mathrm{dens})$ is $-0.0725\pm0.0090$, i.e.\ $8.0\sigma$
over the $4.0$ attained decades. The violation of monotonicity in the fourth
bin is declared and not smoothed; the last column is where it comes from.

That column is the same bins evaluated on the $\sqrt2$ sub-ladder of the same
rung ladder, over the anchor range of the earlier and $20.8$ times smaller node
table, and it carries two readings at once. It is the \emph{node-table}
consistency check: each of the six entries reproduces the value published for
that bin under the smaller table to $0.0\sigma$, which is the sharpest form the
check can take --- with the caveat that the sixth bin ran to $500$ rather than to
$409.6$ there, so the comparison is like-for-like only up to that edge. And it is
the \emph{estimator} dependence, exhibited rather than asserted: the two exponent
columns differ by up to $0.20$, the largest gap in the fourth bin and the next in
the sixth. What differs between them is the rung ladder and the anchor range;
what does not is the node table, so the movement is the estimator and its sample
and not the arithmetic input. That is the caveat of
Remark~\ref{rem:undecidable} as a number.

Two further consistency facts belong to the measurement. \emph{(i)} A larger node
table adds nodes above the old cap and nothing else, so on every window whose
comb was already complete under the old cap the lag vector is unchanged bit for
bit, $R$ is unchanged exactly, and the binned exponent is identical --- a
statement about complete combs, not about tables, and its must-break control is a
window whose comb was truncated under the old cap, which does move.
\emph{(ii)} The two densest bins have no counterpart under the smaller table at
all: they lie beyond the density its cap could reach, which is why they are the
reason for the enlargement.

claims.source_body:
[what the curve does and does not decide, and at what price]
\label{rem:undecidable}
Three statements are part of the claim rather than caveats attached to it.

\emph{Undecidability.} On this surface, a true zero of the binned exponent at
finite density, a power-law approach to zero, and a plateau at any level below
$0.074$ are mutually indistinguishable: $0.074$ is the two-sigma resolution of
the densest bins, and no finite node table reachable under the declared budget
separates the three. No limit is claimed, and the quantifier in
Problem~\ref{prob:R1} is untouched by the curve.

\emph{The resource fence.} The resolution narrows like the square root of the
anchor cap, so the width of the plateau window improves by a factor $2$ for
every factor $4$ in the node table; raising the table by the factor $20.8$ that
produced Surface~III narrowed the window from $0.264$ to $0.074$, a factor
$3.6$. Extending the curve by one further decade of
density needs a node table of about $2.5\cdot10^{9}$, a factor $100$ above the
one used; that is outside the declared budget, and --- this is the honest half
--- it is not obviously the right question either, since the object being
extrapolated is a local slope of a curved surface and not an exponent.

\emph{The ladder caveat.} The estimator of Definition~\ref{def:ratio} is
ladder-dependent. The same density bin evaluated on a $2^{1/4}$ rung ladder and
on its $\sqrt2$ sub-ladder gives different values, with shifts up to $0.20$ on
the surface above, because a bin with about eight rungs samples the curvature of
$\log R$ differently from one with about four. Every number in
Measurement~\ref{meas:density} is therefore quoted \emph{with} its rung ladder,
and a bin value quoted without one is not reproducible.

claims.source_body:
[the value-multiset scramble]
\label{meas:placement}
Replace the node positions $u_\ell$ by sorted uniform samples on the same range,
keeping the weight multiset $\{\varrho_\ell\}$ exactly, and recompute. On $60$
declared draws over the windows of Surface~I:
\begin{itemize}
\item the rank-three collapse is untouched:
  $\sigma_4/\sigma_1\le2.5\cdot10^{-16}$ on every draw, as
  Theorem~\ref{thm:rank3}\ref{R:kernel} requires --- the theorem does not know
  where the nodes are;
\item every majorant of Proposition~\ref{prop:routes} moves by a bounded factor
  and keeps its exponent;
\item the \emph{value} $1-r_{12}^{2}$ moves by a median factor $679$, range
  $26$ to $4.9\cdot10^{3}$. An independent set of draws in the rank module
  gives median $835$, range $69$ to $1.8\cdot10^{4}$; both are quoted, and the
  spread between them is the spread of the sampling.
\end{itemize}
On a second declared surface the same intervention destroys positive
definiteness of the low block on all $24$ draws and moves $R$ by a median
factor $\approx10^{6}$; on the first of the two new density bins of
Surface~III it destroys it on $194/194$ cells with the cell occupancy preserved
exactly, so that only the sub-cell placement is randomised. On Surface~II the
decay is removed outright: over $18$ windows the fitted exponent of
$1-r_{12}^{2}$ moves from $-2.747$ to $+0.009$, a gap of $2.76$ in the
exponent; on a further family the angle $\sin\angle$ rises by a median factor
$6.6\cdot10^{4}$ and its exponent moves from $-1.93$ to $+0.11$. Position and
weight are both load-bearing, and the second is checked separately: keeping the
node positions and replacing each weight by the mean weight gives $h^{-0.116}$
against the true $h^{-2.747}$. The conclusion is
the one sentence this subsection exists for: \emph{every theorem in this paper
survives the scramble and the phenomenon does not}, so the theorems are provably
not where the arithmetic sits. What moves is the joint value of
$(S_{11},S_{22},S_{12})$ against $B$ --- exactly the object
Corollary~\ref{cor:majorant}\ref{M:blind} says no member of $\mathfrak M$ can
see.

claims.source_body:
[the exact placement derivative]
\label{lem:dcexact}
Fix a finite set $F$ of nodes and displace their fractional positions,
$\theta_\ell\mapsto\theta_\ell+\vartheta$ for $\ell\in F$, keeping $m_\ell$ and
all other nodes fixed. As long as no $\theta_\ell+\vartheta$ leaves $[0,1)$, the
lag sequence is affine in $\vartheta$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:dcexact}
  c(\vartheta)=c(0)+\vartheta\,\dot c,
  \qquad
  \dot c=\tfrac12\sum_{\ell\in F}\varrho_\ell
  \bigl(\delta_{m_\ell}-\delta_{m_\ell+1}\bigr),
\end{equation}
where $\delta_m$ is the lag sequence supported at the single lag $m$. In
particular $\dot c$ is exact and piecewise constant in $\vartheta$, and the
induced $\dot A=\Pi^{\T}\Tm{M}(\dot c)\Pi$, $\dot G=\MM^{-1/2}
(t_i^{\T}\dot At_j)_{ij}\MM^{-1/2}$ are exact as well.

claims.source_body:
[causality, the pole, and where the response lives]
\label{meas:pole}
Three numbers on a declared instance family.

\emph{(i) The intervention is causal, and linear over four decades.} Displacing
six declared nodes inside their lag cells --- the cell index fixed, the mass
exactly preserved, twelve lag entries changing --- gives
$\mathrm d\log R/\mathrm d\vartheta=879$, linear to a factor $1.011$ over the
declared range $\vartheta=10^{-7}$ to $10^{-4}$, with an exact
$\vartheta=0$ rebuild control (residual $0$ on $40$ windows). This is a
statement of causation, not of correlation: nothing but the placement was
changed.

\emph{(ii) The number is an identity, not a regression.} On the declared
instance list the closed form \eqref{eq:fh} reproduces the full nonlinear rebuild to
a median relative residual $3.37\cdot10^{-6}$ at the minimum of a declared
central-difference step ladder, with the U-shape exhibited --- round-off limited
below, truncation limited above, both ends at least three times the minimum. A
wrong first-order formula has a floor, not a minimum; two deliberately mutated
formulas (swapped eigenvectors, dropped last term) miss the measured quotient by
a factor of order $40$. Of the three terms of \eqref{eq:fh} the last one, the
near-degeneracy channel, carries the largest share on every instance --- a
median $84\%$, against $7\%$ for the $\lmin$ term.

\emph{(iii) The intervention walks along a near-degeneracy that is already
there.} Sweeping the full placement period on a declared $64$-point grid,
positive definiteness of the low block survives only about $2\%$ of the period:
$\lmin$ changes sign inside the period, so $\log R$ has a \emph{pole} there and
is not defined on the whole period. The bisected loss point satisfies
$\vartheta_{\mathrm{PD}}\cdot|\mathrm d\log R/\mathrm d\vartheta|=5.8$, a pole at
the natural scale, with $\vartheta_{\mathrm{PD}}=5.9\cdot10^{-3}$ median. And
the two lowest modes of the normalised low block already sit only $13.4\%$ apart
at $\vartheta=0$. Consequently a first-harmonic regression of $\log R$ over the
period estimates a Fourier coefficient of a function with a pole in the
interval, and returns $2.89$ against a local derivative of $879$; neither number
is wrong, they measure different things, and the discrepancy is not an anomaly
but a pole.

The cell phases themselves are equidistributed in the classical sense: they are
generated by $\varphi_\ell(h)=\{h\,\theta_\ell\}$ from one real invariant per
node --- an identity certified to $1.14\cdot10^{-13}$ over $1316$ windows and
eight nodes --- and the largest circular-uniformity statistic over those windows
is $1.41$, i.e.\ consistent with uniformity after correction for multiplicity.
Equidistribution of $\{h\theta\}$ is Weyl's theorem \cite{Weyl1916}; it is cited
as the classical address of the phases and is used in no proof.

claims.source_body:
[what is not claimed]
\label{rem:notclaimed}
Problem~\ref{prob:R1} is open. Nothing in this paper bounds it, and nothing in
this paper is conditional on it. Explicitly:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=2.6em]
\item No statement of this paper is an arithmetic statement.
  Theorems~\ref{thm:tvfloor}, \ref{thm:gauge}, \ref{thm:rank3} and every
  proposition, lemma and corollary of
  Sections~\ref{sec:setting}--\ref{sec:rank} hold for an arbitrary finite comb,
  and Measurement~\ref{meas:placement} is the controlled experiment that says
  what changes when the comb does.
\item No fitted exponent is used as a bound. In particular the $\delta$ column
  of Measurement~\ref{meas:routes} certifies nothing beyond the finite surface
  it was fitted on; the inequalities of Proposition~\ref{prop:routes} are the
  proved content of those rows.
\item Measurement~\ref{meas:density} claims no limit. Its explicit content
  includes its own undecidability (Remark~\ref{rem:undecidable}), and the
  quantifier in \eqref{eq:R1} is untouched by it.
\item Positivity of $A$ on the parity sector is used only where it is named as a
  hypothesis, and there only as a per-window certificate.
  Lemma~\ref{lem:detread} exists so that the reduction never needs it.
\item No comparison of a demanded precision against the strength of any
  conjecture appears anywhere in this paper. Problem~\ref{prob:R1} is stated as
  a question about a finite bilinear form and about nothing else.
\end{enumerate}

claims.source_body:
[the floor exponent against the closed exponent]
\label{rem:fit2}
Measurement~\ref{meas:sharpness} reports the floor of
Theorem~\ref{thm:tvfloor} growing as $h^{+1.997}$ on Surface~II, while
\eqref{eq:gap} gives the closed value $1/\mu_1=1/(4\sin^{2}(\pi/N))$ with
$N=2h+1$, whose growth is exactly $h^{2}$ up to the discrete correction. The
two agree, and the small deficit is that correction: expanding the sine,
$1/\mu_1=(2h+1)^{2}/(4\pi^{2})\,(1+O(h^{-2}))$, so a least-squares fit of
$\log(1/\mu_1)$ against $\log h$ over a finite window range returns
$2-c/\log h_{\mathrm{eff}}$ for a positive $c$ coming from the $+1$ in $2h+1$.
The fit is therefore a consistency check on the surface and not an independent
statement; the closed form is what is used, and the fitted number is quoted
because suppressing it would hide the size of the discretisation.

claims.source_body:
[two reported exponents, one measured object]
\label{rem:twoexponents}
Measurement~\ref{meas:rate} reports $h^{-2.747}$ for $1-r_{12}^{2}$ and
$h^{-2.711}$ for the sine of the angle between the rows of $\Ah_2$, on the same
$67$ windows. These are not two independent readings. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:angle} the two quantities differ by the factor
$\ah_{11}\ah_{22}/(\rho_1\rho_2)$, which lies in $(0,1]$ and equals
$\tfrac12$ times the ratio of the geometric to the arithmetic mean of the two
diagonal entries when $r_{12}^{2}$ is close to $1$; the diagonal ratio
$\ah_{22}/\ah_{11}$ stays in a bounded interval on the surface, so the factor
is bounded above and below there and can shift the fitted exponent only by the
slow drift of that ratio. The observed difference, $0.036$ in the exponent, is
of exactly that size. The two numbers are reported because both readings of
Problem~\ref{prob:R1} are in circulation and a reader should be able to match
either; no regression theorem is claimed, and neither number is used as a
bound.

[Hermitian unimodularity]\label{lem:herm}
Define $h(x,y):=\tfrac12\bigl(\ip xy+i\,\ip x{Jy}\bigr)$.  Then $h$ is
a $\Z[i]$-valued Hermitian form on $L$ with $h(x,x)=\tfrac12\ip xx$,
minimum $2$, and $(L,h)$ is \emph{unimodular}: the Hermitian dual of
$L$ is $L$ itself.  Moreover $|(1+J)x|^2=2\,|x|^2$ for all $x$, i.e.\
multiplication by $1+i$ doubles norms exactly.

claims.source_body:
[the Gaussian code bridge, part I: the census]
\label{thm:census}
Let $L=A(\Cst)$ with the $\Z[i]$-structure of
Section~\ref{sec:setup}, and let $(1+i)L=(1+J)L$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $2L\subseteq(1+i)L$, the index is
$[L:(1+i)L]=\det(1+J)=2^4=16=N(1+i)^4$, and
\[
L/(1+i)L\;\cong\;\F_2^4
\]
as an $\F_2$-vector space; the elementary divisors of
$(1+i)L\subseteq L$ are $(1,1,1,1,2,2,2,2)$.
\item[(ii)] \textbf{The zero class is empty on roots}: no root lies
in $(1+i)L$.  Indeed $\min L=4$ by \eqref{eq:douleven}, and by
Lemma~\ref{lem:herm} $\min\,(1+i)L=2\cdot4=8>4$.
\item[(iii)] \textbf{Equidistribution}: each of the $15$ nonzero
classes contains exactly $16$ roots, $240=15\times16$
(finite kernel certificate).
\item[(iv)] \textbf{$\mu_4$-stability}: $Jx\equiv x \bmod (1+i)L$ for
every $x\in L$; in particular every class is $\mu_4$-stable.
\item[(v)] $J$ acts freely on the roots, partitioning them into $60$
\emph{lines} $\{\pm x,\pm Jx\}$ (the Gaussian root lines); each
nonzero class is a union of exactly $4$ lines, $60=15\times4$.
\end{enumerate}

[the Gaussian code bridge, part II: the information
layer]\label{thm:info}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $\bar\sigma^3=1$, $\bar\sigma\neq1$, and the fixed space
of $\bar\sigma$ has dimension $2$ (exactly $4$ fixed labels, $3$ of
them nonzero).
\item[(ii)] On the $15$ root-bearing classes, $\bar\sigma$ acts with
orbit census $3$ fixed classes $+$ $4$ three-cycles.
\item[(iii)] There is a basis $(F_1,F_2,F_3,A)$ of $\F_2^4$ with
\[
\bar\sigma:\ F_1\to F_2\to F_3\to F_1,\qquad \bar\sigma A=A :
\]
$\bar\sigma$ is the \emph{family $3$-cycle with fixed anchor} --- the
information-bit action of the equivariant $\mathrm{RM}(1,3)$
placement, in which each $\mu_4$ pair carries one message bit, the
three moving pairs are the families and the fixed pair is the anchor.
The identification with the $\mathrm{RM}(1,3)$ message space is
unique up to the centralizer of $\bar\sigma$ in $\GL(4,\F_2)$, which
has order exactly $18=|\GL_2(\F_2)|\cdot|\F_4^\times|=6\times3$.
\item[(iv)] \textbf{The coordinate-class law}: the $16$ coordinate
roots $\pm2e_i$ form exactly one class, and that class contains
nothing else; it is $\sigma$-fixed and equals $F_1+F_2+F_3$.  Thus
$240=14\times16+16$ with the coordinate block as the fifteenth
message label, the ``sum of the families''.
\end{enumerate}

claims.source_body:
[quartic invariant restriction, honestly layered]
\label{thm:quartic}
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(Vanishing half: true but trivial.)}  For every
$d\not\equiv0\bmod4$, $F_d|=0$ identically.  Proof: the weight law
$W(J\alpha)=-i\,W(\alpha)$ holds for all $240$ roots, so each
$\mu_4$-orbit $\{\alpha,J\alpha,-\alpha,-J\alpha\}$ contributes
$t^d\bigl(1+(-i)^d+(-1)^d+i^d\bigr)=0$; the orbit factor vanishes if
and only if $d\not\equiv0\bmod4$.  This proves the vanishing of the
degrees $\{2,14,18,30\}$ --- but equally of $6,10,22,26$: the pattern
is $\mu_4$-trivial and carries no $G_{31}$ content.
\item[(b)] \emph{(Isotropy layer: still no $G_{31}$ content.)}
$V^{1,0}$ is $q$-isotropic, and the symbolic $8$-variable identities
\[
f_4=576\,q^2,\qquad f_6=1920\,q^3
\]
hold for the (doubled) root power sums --- $W(E_8)$ has no basic
invariant in degrees $4,6$ --- so $F_4|=F_6|=F_{10}|=0$ on \emph{any}
$q$-isotropic subspace, whether or not the complex structure is
root-compatible (the degree-$10$ case because every degree-$10$
invariant is a combination of $q^5$ and $q f_8$).
\item[(c)] \emph{(The load-bearing content.)}  The restrictions
$F_8|,F_{12}|,F_{20}|,F_{24}|$ are nonzero (exact-point evaluation),
invariant under all $60$ Hermitian reflections and under
$\sigma$ and $J$, and \emph{algebraically independent} (exact Jacobian
$\neq0$).  Since their degrees $(8,12,20,24)$ multiply to
$46080=|G_{31}|$, Chevalley's theorem \cite{Che55,LT09} makes them a
system of \emph{basic invariants} of $G_{31}$: the restriction of the
$W(E_8)$-invariant ring to $V^{1,0}$ generates the full
$G_{31}$-invariant ring.
\item[(d)] \emph{(Jacobian mirror factorization.)}
$\deg\Jac(F_8|,F_{12}|,F_{20}|,F_{24}|)=\sum(d_i-1)=60$, the number
of mirror lines; the Jacobian vanishes at exact generic points on
each of the $60$ mirrors and is nonzero off them, consistent with the
standard factorization $\Jac=c\prod_{60}(\text{mirror forms})$
\cite[Ch.~9]{LT09} --- the full symbolic degree-$60$ expansion was
not performed and is recorded as a named residual.
\end{enumerate}

claims.anchor: \label{sec:status}
requires: Read unabridged original result
Separate identity scope from failed route
Resolve current source version
claims.statement: A failed route and a valid auxiliary identity have different truth statuses. Finite certificates and truncated ledger summaries do not certify full paper coverage.
claims.title: Separate route outcomes from reusable identities

claims.anchor: \label{thm:w1}
requires: Correct Lerch sign and origin scheme
Explicit pole and rebinning corrections
Bounds on the actual test domain
claims.statement: The source distinguishes measure identities, tent and B-spline reads, pole corrections, origin conventions and rebinning. A scalar identification without the stated corrections is not an exact full-domain positivity transfer.
claims.title: W1 measure dictionary with convention lock

claims.anchor: \label{lem:proj}
requires: H1_0 boundary conditions
Explicit parity reduction or full test coverage
claims.statement: Mean zero of derivatives of H1_0 tests is automatic; oddness of the undifferentiated tests is an additional sector restriction. These are not the same full-domain coverage statement.
claims.title: W1 differentiated mean-zero versus odd test sector

claims.anchor: \label{thm:structure}
requires: Valid full explicit formula
Complex-frequency contributions and tail
No critical-line assumption in construction
claims.statement: The finite window admits a zero-side alias-comb reading with pole terms. Nonnegativity on real frequencies does not establish that every relevant zero has real frequency.
claims.title: W3 signed alias-comb identity

claims.anchor: \label{sec:c1}
requires: Lock direction only
Independent low-zero sampling budget
No upgrade from average to supremum
claims.statement: The C=1 discussion is confined to the pole-killed lock direction. The full-space operator reading is rejected; density averages alone do not establish the required supremum budget.
claims.title: C=1 is direction-specific, not an operator bound

claims.anchor: \label{lem:fejer}
requires: Admissible smoothing width
Unconditional treatment of complex zero frequencies
Uniform remainder and resolution control
claims.statement: Fejer smoothing connects the symbol to the zero density. Smoothing-width restrictions, off-line contributions and tail control must remain explicit; a smoothed bound is not pointwise positivity.
claims.title: Fejer smoothing does not provide arbitrary resolution

documents.title: W3: alias detector and smoothing limits

claims.anchor: \label{sec:conclusion}
requires: Tightness proved on the growing family
Compatible operator domains
Zero-independent signed trace identity
Independent cofinal positivity
claims.statement: Finite states and measured spectral convergence do not supply a global Hilbert–Polya operator. Tightness, spectral identification, compatible limits and independent positivity retain their own proof obligations.
claims.title: HP limit needs more than finite spectral matches

claims.anchor: \subsection{Lean anchors}
requires: Fresh type and axiom audit for selected declarations
Paper-to-declaration domain match
Global bridge separately proved
claims.statement: The paper names 116 public theorem declarations in four finite-algebra modules. Source discovery is not fresh kernel validation or an automatic proof of the paper's measurement and limit layers.
claims.title: Four Lean modules are finite algebraic anchors

claims.anchor: Every load-bearing claim below is typed
requires: Separate symbolic identity, rational certificate and floating residual
Certified error control where numerical
claims.statement: The paper's PROVED convention includes finite floating-point residuals. Importing this label as a machine-checked mathematical theorem would conflate different evidence standards.
claims.title: Paper PROVED labels are not kernel certificates

claims.anchor: \label{thm:rung}
requires: Fine matrix positive definite
Exact nesting
U positive definite and certified majorant
Carried coarse solution
claims.statement: The rung bounds delta by shat-transpose times inverse-U times shat. It assumes fine-level positive definiteness, exact nesting and a certified positive majorant, and uses the carried coarse solution.
claims.title: Certified rung with all H1–H3 premises

claims.anchor: \label{cor:chain}
requires: Actual-family nonvanishing or independent strict base
Do not mistake arbitrary matrices for admissible arithmetic windows
claims.statement: The rung permits zero residual, while the chain proof invokes strictly positive rung contributions. A nonvanishing argument for the actual admissible family must be supplied before importing this strict conclusion.
claims.title: Chain strictness needs nonvanishing review

claims.anchor: \label{L:uniform}
requires: Source-pure base case
All new Schur-complement inequalities
Cofinal admissible family
Full test-class coverage
claims.statement: Window-by-window Cholesky results do not prove a cofinal family. The new Schur complements, admissible domains and residual increments require control at every needed level; a fixed positive margin is not presumed.
claims.title: Multilevel continuation beyond finite certificates

claims.anchor: \label{L:secondroute}
requires: Increment sign theorem
Summed Harnack ratio bound
Actual inverse and domain identification
claims.statement: The paper names a separate corner route requiring sign and summed Harnack-type ratio control of inverse increments. Observations on sampled windows do not supply those assumptions uniformly.
claims.title: Unproved alternative inverse-corner route

claims.anchor: \label{thm:tvfloor}
requires: Specified parity basis and spectral gap
Original lag-weight definition
claims.statement: The total-variation floor uses the exact admissibility normalization x_1=1 and the parity spectral gap. It is not a no-go for arbitrary normalization or unrestricted vectors.
claims.title: Normalized total-variation floor

claims.anchor: \label{thm:rank3}
requires: Exact symmetric two-by-two block
Signed pole/archimedean convention
Joint arithmetic control of all three functionals
claims.statement: The comb–comb determinant depends on three linear functionals. Compression does not bound their joint position relative to the archimedean block and does not itself prove positivity.
claims.title: Rank-three compression preserves joint arithmetic data

claims.anchor: \item\label{R:inertia}
requires: Claim restricted to the printed universal arbitrary-P sentence
claims.statement: For J with signature (1,2), P=((1,0),(-1,0),(0,1)) gives P-transpose J P / 2 = -I_2. Rank two alone does not imply indefiniteness; the rank and inertia upper bounds remain valid.
claims.title: Universal rank-two indefiniteness is false

claims.anchor: \label{prob:R1}
requires: Uniform window-dependent arithmetic estimate
Diagonal normalization control
Separate any intended implication to RH
claims.statement: The uniform rate for 1-r_12 squared is an open joint-cancellation problem. Neither the observed rate nor an asserted RH equivalence is supplied by this paper.
claims.title: R1 joint normalized determinant rate

claims.anchor: Honest scope of the formal layer
requires: Quotient identification if needed
Root-list completeness
External invariant-theory premises
claims.statement: Lean covers explicit Smith maps, matrices and a fixed root list. The actual quotient-module construction, root-list completeness and parts of the invariant-theory identification remain separate from those finite certificates.
claims.title: Gaussian finite certificates do not formalize every identification

claims.anchor: \label{sec:scope}
requires: Input-dependent arithmetic action
Signed all-place identity
Compatible growing carrier and independent positivity
claims.statement: The Gaussian-code paper asserts finite algebra and explicitly no arithmetic or RH consequence. A finite code alone does not realize the full signed Weil form.
claims.title: Finite Gaussian code needs an independent arithmetic bridge
